Supervised Bayesian factor models for molecular programs and survival in pancreatic cancer

Technical report on the evaluated methods, current evidence, and remaining work

Author

Andrew J. Walther

Published

October 14, 2026

Status: initial draft awaiting independent review. This report describes methods and evidence available through October 12, 2026. It has not yet been reviewed independently, and it is not ready to share beyond the immediate project team. Every quantitative statement is traced to a saved output in paper/writeup/source_inventory.csv; claims that could not be traced are omitted or listed as evidence gaps. The planned manuscript authors are Walther, Liu, and Rashid. DeSurv (Young et al. 2026) is cited throughout as the source of the gene-screening rule and the published factor gene lists.

Summary of current findings

What the models are. Both models factor molecular data into nonnegative patient activities \(L\) and feature loadings \(F\), and link survival to the observable projection of each patient’s data onto the loadings, \(\eta = (YF)\beta\). The single-modality model fits one feature block. The multimodal model shares \(L\) across matched expression and methylation blocks, adds per-feature intercepts and signed loadings, and propagates loading uncertainty into its coefficient updates.

What the evaluated single-modality configuration does. In the configuration behind all single-modality results (\(\alpha_F = 0\)), survival informs the coefficients \(\beta\) but not the loadings \(F\) or the activities \(L\). The programs are therefore the programs of an empirical-Bayes factorization of the training data; survival selects and weights them. This is not the intended final method (Section 5.4).

Single-modality performance. Trained on TCGA-PAAD RNA-seq and CPTAC proteomics (\(n = 273\)), the frozen model has a mean concordance of 0.627 across five held-out cohorts (\(n = 616\)). Against an independently tuned two-step comparator (40 unsupervised factors, LASSO Cox), the C-index difference computed on the 616 concatenated patients is 0.026 (95% bootstrap interval 0.000 to 0.050). Against a two-step comparator given the same rank of 7 the difference is 0.011 (\(-0.013\) to \(0.033\)).

Single-modality biology. Starting from rank 7, four programs are retained and two are classified as survival-active. The adverse program (7) aligns with the basal-like axis and the protective program (3) with the classical axis; the two genomics-only programs read as desmoplastic stroma (5) and immune infiltrate with a vascular component (6). These labels rest on enrichment, subtype concordance and gene-list overlap analyses that share inputs and were not prespecified.

Multimodal model. In simulation, the framework with intercepts, signed loadings, empirical-Bayes priors and evidence-based pruning returns close to the true rank of 3 from every starting rank at moderate noise, and converges in all 162 of its fits. It does not recover a planted low-variance prognostic program at moderate noise. On real data, nothing is pruned at any starting rank, most fits reach the 500-sweep cap, and external concordance on 50 primary-PDAC ICGC donors varies from 0.50 to 0.69 across starting ranks. At starting rank 7 the joint fit has \(C = 0.685\) and the expression-only fit of the same framework \(C = 0.676\); both are unconverged. Methylation adds a methylation-dominant program and loads on an immune program; it does not demonstrably improve prediction.

Main open problems. Survival-guided discovery of programs, a rank-selection rule that accounts for both survival and reconstruction on real data, full convergence of real multimodal fits, feature-count sensitivity, matched comparisons with DeSurv and unsupervised factorization, and a methylation-specific biological interpretation (Section 5.2).

1 Methods

1.1 Notation

Patients are indexed by \(i = 1, \dots, n\), molecular features by \(j\), factors (programs) by \(k = 1, \dots, K\), and data blocks (modalities) by \(m\). Patient \(i\) has observed time \(t_i\) and event indicator \(\delta_i\) (1 for death, 0 for censoring). The single-modality data are an \(n \times p\) matrix \(Y\); the multimodal data are matched blocks \(Y_m\) of dimension \(n \times p_m\), here expression (\(m = \mathrm{expr}\)) and DNA methylation (\(m = \mathrm{meth}\)). Methylation measurements are written \(Y_{\mathrm{meth}}\); the symbol \(\beta\) is reserved for survival coefficients.

Three patient-level quantities must be kept apart: the latent activities \(L \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n \times K}\), posterior scores in the reconstruction \(Y \approx LF^\top\), defined only for training patients; the projection scores, the observable product of a patient’s data with the posterior-mean loadings, which enter the Cox predictor and can be computed for new patients (\(\tilde Z\) in Equation 2, \(Z\) in Equation 5); and the signature scores used only in biological characterization, the mean of within-cohort z-scored expression over a selected gene set.

1.2 Single-modality model

Reconstruction and priors. The training matrix is modeled as \[ y_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^K L_{ik} F_{jk} + e_{ij}, \qquad e_{ij} \sim N(0, \tau_j^{-1}), \tag{1}\] with independent point-exponential priors \(L_{ik} \sim g_{L,k}\) and \(F_{jk} \sim g_{F,k}\) (a point mass at zero mixed with an exponential distribution), whose parameters are estimated by empirical Bayes within each factor using the ebnm package. Each feature has its own residual precision \(\tau_j\), estimated by maximum likelihood.

Survival predictor. Survival follows a Cox model whose linear predictor is the normalized projection of the patient’s data onto the posterior-mean loadings: \[ \eta_i = \sum_{k=1}^K \tilde Z_{ik}\tilde\beta_k, \qquad \tilde Z = Y \bar F D^{-1}, \quad D = \mathrm{diag}\big(\lVert \bar F_{\cdot 1}\rVert_2, \dots, \lVert \bar F_{\cdot K}\rVert_2\big). \tag{2}\] Each column of \(\bar F D^{-1}\) has unit Euclidean length, so \(\tilde Z_{ik}\) is the coordinate of \(y_i\) along program \(k\)’s loading direction. The normalization keeps \(\tilde Z\) on a scale that does not grow with \(p\); without it, coefficient shrinkage drove every \(\tilde\beta_k\) to zero (S04). The coefficients \(\tilde\beta_k\) have independent normal priors with zero mean and a variance estimated per factor, so they are interpreted per unit of normalized projection, not per standard deviation. Because \(\tilde Z\) depends only on \(Y\) and \(\bar F\), the same formula scores training and new patients.

Cox working approximation. The Cox partial likelihood is replaced at each sweep by a second-order expansion around the current predictor \(\hat\eta\) with a diagonal Breslow curvature, \[ \log \mathrm{PL}(\eta) \approx \mathrm{const} - \tfrac12 \sum_i w_i (z_i - \eta_i)^2, \qquad w_i = \hat\theta_i \hat H_0(t_i), \quad z_i = \hat\eta_i + (\delta_i - w_i)/w_i, \tag{3}\] where \(\hat\theta_i = \exp(\hat\eta_i)\) and \(\hat H_0\) is the Breslow cumulative baseline hazard. Off-diagonal curvature is dropped. Appendix A derives each coordinate update from this surrogate.

Where survival enters. Two weights appear in the implementation. The survival weight \(\alpha \in [0,1]\) multiplies the survival term in the coefficient update; the evaluated value is \(\alpha = 0.5\), which leaves the pseudo-observation \(B/A\) unchanged and halves its precision. The loading weight \(\alpha_F\) mixes a reconstruction contribution, with weight \(1 - \alpha_F\), and a survival contribution, with weight \(\alpha_F\), in the update of \(F\). The evaluated configuration uses \(\alpha_F = 0\). The activities \(L\) do not appear in \(\eta\), so their update is a reconstruction update in every configuration. Consequently, in the evaluated fits survival determines \(\tilde\beta\) but not \(L\) or \(F\); it affects which programs are scored as prognostic, not what the programs are. The coefficient update also treats \(\tilde Z\) as fixed: it does not propagate posterior uncertainty in \(F\) (Table 12).

1.3 Single-modality fitting algorithm and prediction

NoteAlgorithm 1. Evaluated single-modality fit (fit_cox_on_yf(), configuration D4)

Input: standardized training matrix \(Y\) (\(n = 273\), \(p = 2{,}064\)), \((t_i, \delta_i)\), starting rank \(K = 7\), \(\alpha = 0.5\), \(\alpha_F = 0\), normal coefficient prior.

  1. Initialize \(\bar L, \bar F\) from the absolute values of the leading \(K\) singular vectors of \(Y\) scaled by \(\sqrt{d_k}\); set \(\tilde\beta = 0\) and \(\tau_j = 1/\widehat{\mathrm{var}}(y_{\cdot j})\).
  2. For each outer iteration (at most 300):
    1. Form \(D\) and \(\tilde Z = Y\bar F D^{-1}\); compute \(\eta = \tilde Z\bar{\tilde\beta}\) and the working quantities \((w, z)\) of Equation 3. These are held fixed for the rest of the iteration.
    2. For \(k = 1, \dots, K\):
      1. update \(q(\tilde\beta_k)\) from \(A = \alpha\sum_i w_i \tilde Z_{ik}^2\) and \(B = \alpha\sum_i w_i \tilde Z_{ik}(z_i - \eta_{i,-k})\) by empirical-Bayes normal means with pseudo-observation \(x = B/A\) and standard error \(A^{-1/2}\);
      2. update \(q(L_{\cdot k})\) from the reconstruction residual excluding factor \(k\) (no survival term);
      3. update \(q(F_{\cdot k})\) from the reconstruction residual only (\(\alpha_F = 0\)).
    3. Update \(\tau_j = n / \sum_i E(y_{ij} - L_i^\top F_j)^2\).
    4. Compute the monitoring objective \(J = (1-\alpha)G + \alpha p S - \mathrm{KL}\) (Appendix A.8). Stop after iteration 5 if \(|\Delta J|/|J| < 10^{-5}\).
  3. Orientation. Compare the training concordance of \(\eta\) with 0.5 and, if needed, negate \(\bar{\tilde\beta}\) once. The saved D4 fit predates the September 4 correction of this check, so its \(\eta\) is a good-prognosis score; it is scored as \(\mathrm{risk} = -\eta\) for every held-out cohort (Section 1.3.1).
  4. Classify factors (Section 1.4).

Output: \(\bar L\), \(\bar F\), \(D\), \(\bar{\tilde\beta}\), \(\tau\). Prediction: for a new patient with standardized data \(y_{\mathrm{new}}\) restricted to the training genes that are measured, \(\mathrm{risk}_{\mathrm{new}} = -\,y_{\mathrm{new}}^\top \bar F D^{-1}\bar{\tilde\beta}\), with all quantities fixed from training.

The saved D4 fit met the stopping rule at iteration 20 (S04, S58). The monitoring objective weights the reconstruction and survival terms by \(1-\alpha\) and \(\alpha p\); it is used to decide when to stop and is not the evidence lower bound of a single generative model. The coefficient posterior variances stored with this historical fit equal zero to machine precision, consistent with the pre-September sign-correction code, which overwrote \(E(\tilde\beta^2)\) with \(E(\tilde\beta)^2\) when it negated the coefficients (S01, 2026-09-04 entry). The report therefore gives no coefficient uncertainty for this fit.

1.3.1 Risk orientation

A concordance index requires a direction: which end of the score indicates higher risk. That direction must be fixed from training data alone; choosing it in each validation cohort from that cohort’s outcomes would bias the index upward. For the saved D4 fit, \(\eta = \tilde Z\tilde\beta\) is concordant with longer survival, and make_km_figures.R and run_external_ci_analysis.R use the single global convention \(\mathrm{risk} = -\eta\) for all held-out cohorts (S01, S49). On the risk scale, the coefficient of Program 7 is \(+0.040\) and that of Program 3 is \(-0.012\). This convention is specific to the historical saved fit and is not a rule for current fits, whose orientation step was corrected on September 4.

1.4 Programs, starting rank, and classification

Three counts must be kept apart. The starting rank \(K_{\mathrm{init}}\) is the number of factors at initialization. A factor is survival-active if \(|\bar{\tilde\beta}_k| > 0.001\). A factor that is not survival-active is genomics-only if its proportion of variance explained, \(\mathrm{PVE}_k = \lVert \bar L_{\cdot k}\rVert^2 \lVert \bar F_{\cdot k}\rVert^2 / \lVert Y \rVert_F^2\), exceeds 1%, and dead otherwise. The retained molecular programs are the survival-active and genomics-only factors together. In the single-modality model this is a classification of one fitted model: no factor is removed and nothing is refitted. The two thresholds are operational. The coefficient threshold was set from the observed scale of \(\tilde\beta\) in this model (S37), and neither threshold is a posterior probability.

The starting rank of 7 has two sources. It was first chosen by five-fold cross-validated training concordance with a one-standard-error rule: the best mean was at \(K = 8\) (0.651, SE 0.026), and \(K = 7\) was the smallest rank within one standard error (0.633; S55). It was retained after a sweep over \(K_{\mathrm{init}} = 2, \dots, 20\) in which the criteria disagreed (Section 3.3). External concordance in the five held-out cohorts reaches a plateau at \(K_{\mathrm{init}} = 7\), and that plateau was part of the evidence for keeping 7. The recommendation is therefore not purely training-selected.

1.5 Multiple cohorts in the single-block model

The established model fits one feature block pooled from two training cohorts on different platforms: TCGA-PAAD RNA-seq (\(n = 144\)) and CPTAC mass-spectrometry proteomics (\(n = 129\)). CPTAC is a proteomics cohort, not a second RNA-seq cohort (S03). Genes are screened separately in each cohort by the DeSurv combined mean-and-variance rank (Young et al. 2026), keeping the top 3,000 per cohort; the intersection has 2,064 genes. Each cohort is then standardized gene by gene to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (per-platform standardization). Held-out cohorts receive the same per-platform standardization and are scored on the training genes they measure.

Three optional cohort terms are distinct model components: cohort_id adds cohort indicator columns to \(L\) (a genomic offset), strata_id forms Cox risk sets within cohort (a cohort-specific baseline hazard), and beta_cohort_id gives each cohort its own partially pooled coefficients. The recommended configuration uses none of them; the decision record reports the last two as performance-neutral externally (S01).

1.6 Multimodal model

Reconstruction. For matched blocks \(m \in \{\mathrm{expr}, \mathrm{meth}\}\), \[ Y_m = \mathbf{1}\mu_m^\top + L F_m^\top + E_m, \qquad (E_m)_{ij} \sim N(0, \tau_{mj}^{-1}), \tag{4}\] with a feature intercept \(\mu_m\) re-estimated at each outer sweep, shared nonnegative activities \(L\) (point-exponential prior per factor), modality-specific signed loadings \(F_m\) with a point-Laplace prior \(g_{mk}\) for each modality and factor, and feature-specific precisions \(\tau_{mj}\). The intercept is what makes signed loadings appropriate: \(F_m\) describes deviations from each feature’s baseline, and \(L\) remains interpretable as program activity. Prior parameters for \(L\) and \(F_m\) are estimated by marginal likelihood after each sweep, so a whole column can shrink to the point mass at zero.

Survival predictor. With \(\tilde Y_m = Y_m - \mathbf{1}\mu_m^\top\), the joint projection and predictor are \[ Z = \sum_m \tilde Y_m F_m, \qquad \eta_i = \sum_k Z_{ik}\beta_k, \qquad \beta_k \sim N(0, \sigma_k^2). \tag{5}\] The projection is not normalized; instead, after every factor update, \((L_{\cdot k}, F_{mk}, \beta_k)\) is replaced by \((c_k L_{\cdot k}, F_{mk}/c_k, c_k\beta_k)\) with \(c_k = \mathrm{sd}(Z_{\cdot k})\), which leaves both \(L F_m^\top\) and \(\eta\) unchanged and fixes \(\mathrm{sd}(Z_{\cdot k}) = 1\) in training. This canonicalization removes the scale direction along which survival and reconstruction terms can otherwise drift (S01, 2026-10-02 entry). Posterior second moments and prior rates are transformed under the same change of variables. A constant shift of \(\eta\) leaves the partial likelihood unchanged, so the intercept does not affect the survival term.

Updates. The loading update adds reconstruction and Cox working terms with equal weight and couples features through the projection, so features are updated one at a time with the projection moments refreshed after each. The coefficient update uses \(E(Z_{ik}^2) = E(Z_{ik})^2 + \mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik})\), so loading uncertainty shrinks the coefficient. Appendix B gives the derivations.

Evidence and factor removal. The objective used for factor removal is \[ \mathcal{E} = \sum_{m,j}\Big[\tfrac n2 \log\tfrac{\hat\tau_{mj}}{2\pi} - \tfrac{\hat\tau_{mj}}2 E\lVert \tilde y_{mj} - L f_{mj}\rVert^2\Big] + \log \mathrm{PL}\big(E(\eta)\big) - \mathrm{KL}(q\,\Vert\, g), \tag{6}\] with \(\hat\tau\) at its maximum-likelihood value. The survival term is the partial log-likelihood at the posterior mean predictor (a plug-in), not its expectation under \(q\). After the coordinate loop, the change in \(\mathcal{E}\) from deleting each factor is computed with the other factors fixed and the intercept and precisions re-estimated; if a deletion does not lower \(\mathcal{E}\), the factor with the largest gain is removed and the model refitted, repeatedly. The check runs whether or not the loop converged (S08).

Classification. A factor is reconstruction-active if its share of total sum of squares, \(\sum_m\lVert \bar L_{\cdot k}\bar F_{mk}^\top\rVert_F^2 / \sum_m\lVert\tilde Y_m\rVert_F^2\), is at least 1%, and survival-active if \(|E\beta_k|/\mathrm{sd}(\beta_k) \ge 1.96\). These are reported separately from removal.

1.7 Multimodal fitting algorithm

NoteAlgorithm 2. Evaluated multimodal fit (fit_multimodal_yfb(), pruned framework)

Input: raw training blocks \(Y_m\) (log2 expression, methylation \(\beta\)-values), \((t_i, \delta_i)\), starting rank \(K_{\mathrm{init}}\). Controls: intercept on; point-Laplace loading priors; marginal-likelihood prior updates; feature-specific maximum-likelihood \(\tau\); plug-in survival term; pruning on; at most 500 outer sweeps of 5 inner sweeps; tolerance \(10^{-4}\).

  1. Initialize \(\mu_m\) at column means; \(\bar L\) and \(\bar F_m\) from absolute singular vectors of the concatenated centered blocks; \(\tau_{mj}\) from the pooled variance of each block; \(\beta\) from a Cox fit on standardized initial projections, transformed back to the raw projection scale.
  2. For each outer sweep (at most 500):
    1. Re-estimate \(\mu_m\) and re-center \(\tilde Y_m\). Compute \(E(Z)\), \(\mathrm{Var}(Z)\), \(E(\eta)\), and the Cox working quantities \(w_i\) and \(h_i = u_i + w_i E(\eta_i)\); hold \((w, h)\) fixed for this outer sweep.
    2. Repeat 5 inner sweeps; for \(k = 1, \dots, K\):
      1. update \(q(L_{\cdot k})\) from both blocks’ reconstruction residuals; refit its point-exponential prior;
      2. for each modality, update \(q(f_{mjk})\) feature by feature with reconstruction and survival terms, refreshing \(E(Z_{\cdot k})\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Z_{\cdot k})\) after each feature; refit the point-Laplace prior \(g_{mk}\);
      3. update \(q(\beta_k)\) with \(A = \sum_i w_i E(Z_{ik}^2)\), \(B = \sum_i E(Z_{ik}) h_{i,-k}\), and prior variance \(\sigma_k^2 = \max(0, B^2/A^2 - 1/A)\);
      4. canonicalize factor \(k\) so that \(\mathrm{sd}(Z_{\cdot k}) = 1\).
    3. Update \(\tau_{mj} = n / E\lVert\tilde y_{mj} - L f_{mj}\rVert^2\).
    4. Stop if the maximum relative change in each fitted reconstruction \(\bar L\bar F_m^\top\) and in \(E(\eta)\) is below \(10^{-4}\).
  3. Removal check. Compute the change in Equation 6 from deleting each factor; if the largest change is \(\ge 0\), delete that factor, refit from the remaining factors (returning to step 2 with a warm start), and repeat.

Output: posterior moments, priors, \(\mu_m\), \(\tau\), classification. Prediction: \(\mathrm{risk}_{\mathrm{new}} = \sum_m y_{m,\mathrm{new}}^\top\bar F_m\bar\beta\), with orientation fixed from training (flip = FALSE). Centering new data at the training intercept would change every score by the same constant and leave the C-index unchanged.

1.8 Approximations and what the objectives do not guarantee

Each coordinate update is exact for the quadratic Cox surrogate at fixed working quantities, but the surrogate changes between sweeps, its curvature is diagonal, the single-modality monitor reweights its components, and the multimodal removal objective evaluates survival at \(E(\eta)\). Neither algorithm is therefore exact coordinate ascent on one evidence lower bound, and neither is guaranteed to increase monotonically. Appendices A and B list each approximation beside the update it affects.

The evaluated single-modality configuration with \(\alpha_F = 0\) is a stage in the development of the method, not its intended final form. Planned work on survival supervision of the loadings, coefficient priors, and rank selection is described in one place, Section 5.4.

2 Evaluation framework

2.1 Simulation designs

Single-modality, multiple cohorts (S17, S18, S59). Each dataset has two cohorts of 150 patients and 1,000 genes. True loading columns are the absolute values of unsupervised factorization programs estimated from the real training data, scaled to amplitude 12; feature noise precisions are drawn from Gamma(2, 2). Survival times follow a Weibull proportional-hazards model with predictor \(\sum_k L_{ik}\beta_k\) over the shared programs (coefficients recycled from \(1.5, -1.2, 0.8, -0.5\)), and censoring is calibrated to 30%. Study-specific programs have zero loadings outside their cohort and no survival effect. Three scenarios vary the structure: all shared (six shared programs), hybrid (two shared and two specific per cohort), and nothing shared (three specific per cohort, so no program is prognostic). Each dataset is split 75/25 into training and test patients, stratified by event status. Two arms are fitted at starting ranks 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, and 20 with 15 seeds, giving 540 fits: the single-modality model with the evaluated settings, and a two-step arm consisting of a nonnegative empirical-Bayes factorization (flashier, at most \(K_{\mathrm{init}}\) factors, backfitted) followed by an unpenalized Cox model on least-squares projection scores. Note that the data-generating predictor uses the latent activities \(L\), whereas the model predicts from projections \(YF\).

Multimodal (S25, S26, S59). Each dataset has 120 training and 120 validation patients, 50 expression and 50 methylation features, and three true programs. Survival follows a Weibull model with predictor \(\sum_m Y_m F_m \beta\), matching the model’s predictor form. Three scenarios set \(\beta\): two prognostic programs (\(0.70, 0.35, 0\)), adverse and protective (\(0.70, -0.70, 0\)), and a low-variance prognostic program whose activities are scaled by 0.15 (\(\beta = 0, 0, 1.10\)). Noise is set by a multiplier on every feature’s noise standard deviation: 1 reproduces the September design and 0.25 is lower noise (“moderate”). Each feature is shifted by four noise standard deviations so the data are nonnegative and the original model can be fitted. Starting ranks are 3–10 and 15, with three seeds per setting. Three variants are fitted to every dataset: the original September model (no intercept, nonnegative loadings, moment prior updates, no pruning), the evaluated pruned framework (Algorithm 2), and the same framework with the variance-corrected survival term. The full sweep contains 486 fits, 162 per variant.

2.2 Data

The matched multimodal cohorts are built from the TCGA and ICGC files with expression and methylation for the same patients (S30). Methylation is restricted to the 305,352 CpGs present in both cohorts’ sex-chromosome-filtered probe sets; missing values (0.07% in TCGA) are imputed within cohort by \(k\)-nearest neighbors. The evaluated multimodal fits use raw inputs: log2 expression and methylation \(\beta\)-values. Screening uses training data only.

2.3 Comparators and prediction rules

Principal single-modality comparator. An unsupervised empirical-Bayes factorization (flashier, signed point-normal priors, gene-specific variances, greedy fitting with backfitting, at most 40 factors) of the same \(273 \times 2{,}064\) training matrix, followed by a LASSO Cox model on projection scores \(Y\bar F D^{-1}\) with the penalty chosen by cross-validation (lambda.min). The factor count was not informed by the supervised model; 15 of the 40 factors received nonzero coefficients (S10). Held-out patients are scored with the frozen loadings and coefficients.

Supporting single-modality comparators. A rank-matched two-step model (7 factors, unpenalized Cox; S12) and the earlier comparator (20 factors, unpenalized Cox; S13). Matching the rank gives the two-step model the supervised model’s answer about complexity, and the unpenalized 20-factor model is not regularized; neither is the principal comparison. The output directory desurv_comparison contains our own models fitted with DeSurv-aligned and alternative preprocessing (configurations D1–D5); it is not a fitted DeSurv benchmark (S48).

Multimodal comparators. On the matched cohorts, the same framework fitted to expression alone (configuration pruned_expression_only) isolates the contribution of methylation. Two further arms are reported for completeness: an older isolated single-modality fitter on raw log2 expression (expression_only_yfb, which is not the expression-only fit of the evaluated framework) and two-step factorization followed by Cox on stacked or expression-only data (S28). The established single-modality model was trained on different data and preprocessing and is discussed separately (Section 3.5).

2.4 Performance metrics and uncertainty

External performance is Harrell’s concordance index with a risk orientation fixed from training. All per-cohort single-modality values in Table 3 were re-computed during drafting from the saved risk scores with frozen orientation and agree with the saved values to four decimals (S56); some of the saved runners had computed the outcome-oriented \(\max(C, 1 - C)\), which coincides with the frozen value in every cohort here. Confidence intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals over patients (\(B = 2{,}000\) for single-modality, \(1{,}000\) for multimodal; seed 1).

Three summaries of the single-modality comparison are not interchangeable: the mean external C averages five cohort C-indices; the concatenated difference (principal and rank-matched comparisons) computes one C-index per model over all 616 patients, so comparable pairs cross cohorts, with an unstratified bootstrap; and the inverse-variance pooled difference (older comparator) combines per-cohort paired differences. None is an equivalence or non-inferiority test.

Simulation summaries are means over seeds. In the single-modality simulation, test-set concordance is the outcome-oriented \(\max(C, 1-C)\) (S17), which is biased upward when there is no signal: in the nothing-shared scenario both arms score about 0.54. In the multimodal simulation, validation concordance uses the frozen orientation. Program recovery is the absolute correlation between a true loading column and its best-matching estimated column; a program counts as recovered at \(|r| \ge 0.7\).

2.5 Biological characterization methods

The biological labels in Section 4 come from existing analyses of the established single-modality fit and of the starting-rank-7 multimodal fit. Table 14 in Appendix C lists, for each analysis, the object analysed, the population, the statistic and settings, the multiplicity scope, and what the output can support. No analysis in this table was rerun for this report.

Several of these analyses share inputs and are not independent validations. The custom fgsea collection and the gene-list overlap both use DeSurv’s lists, and the selected gene universe was itself screened with DeSurv’s rule. The subtype concordance uses training activities \(E(L)\) in TCGA, which also trained the model. The original external signature check (C2) scored each program’s lowest-padj set; for Program 6 that set was the DeSurv classical-tumor list, the same list used as Program 3’s signature, so C2 measured the classical axis rather than Program 6. The corrected control (C4) excludes the entire PDAC_custom collection, including the Moffitt and Bailey lists, and was designed after C2’s result; it is a post hoc correction. Multiple-testing control is within program and collection only. The pathway report itself states that these methods were chosen for availability rather than from a review of what the question requires and that the choice warrants assessment before manuscript use (S21). Two further cautions apply to the signature helper: its hazard ratio is per unit of the mean z-scored signature, not per standard deviation, and its concordance output is \(\max(C, 1-C)\), which is outcome-oriented and cannot substitute for frozen-risk validation. Those concordance values are not used in this report.

3 Results

3.1 Single-modality simulation

Table 15 and Figure 5 in Appendix C summarize the 540 fits. At or above the true rank (6), the model recovers every shared program at \(|r| \ge 0.7\) and nearly every study-specific program, and over-specifying the rank to 12 or 20 changes little. The two-step arm recovers fewer programs and stops changing beyond rank 6 because its greedy factorization stops adding factors. The model’s test concordance exceeds the two-step arm’s by about 0.10 in the hybrid scenario from rank 3 upward and by about 0.02 in the all-shared scenario from rank 6; with nothing prognostic both are near the outcome-oriented null of 0.54. With \(\alpha_F = 0\) the model’s \(L\) and \(F\) updates ignore survival, so these differences come from the fitting procedure (singular-vector initialization and coordinate updates versus greedy flashier), not from survival supervision. Possible merges, an estimate correlated above 0.5 with two true programs, occurred in a single-seed diagnostic only at starting ranks 2–4 (S19). Among programs without a survival effect, 22%–35% were classified survival-active in the hybrid scenario and 6%–10% with nothing shared.

A separate ten-seed simulation tested cohort-specific coefficients for a program that is prognostic in only one cohort (S20). The coefficient in the owning cohort exceeded the other cohort’s in 15 of 20 cohort-by-seed cases at starting rank 6 and 17 of 20 at rank 12 (medians 0.060 versus 0.008, and 0.054 versus 0.008); one seed diverged, so medians are the reported summary.

3.2 Single-modality external validation

Table 3 gives per-cohort concordance. The frozen model’s mean external C is 0.627 (0.549 in Moffitt to 0.657 in PACA-AU RNA-seq) and the principal comparator’s 0.601. Over the 616 concatenated patients the C-indices are 0.629 and 0.603, a difference of 0.026 with 95% interval 0.000 to 0.050; the lower limit is 0.0002, so the advantage is marginal (S11, S56, S60). The rank-matched comparator, which is better in both PACA-AU cohorts, gives a difference of 0.011 (\(-0.013\) to \(0.033\); S12). The older unpenalized comparator gives 0.042 (0.013 to 0.071), with a per-cohort interval excluding zero only in Puleo (S13).

Within each cohort, patients were split into tertiles of the frozen risk score (Figure 1). The low-risk tertile has the longest survival in every cohort; the log-rank test has \(p < 0.05\) in Dijk (\(p = 0.00046\)), PACA-AU RNA-seq (\(0.021\)), and Puleo (\(< 0.0001\)), and not in PACA-AU array (\(0.075\)) or Moffitt (\(0.17\)) (S36). Tertiles are within-cohort descriptive groups, not fixed clinical cutoffs.

3.3 Starting rank and factor classification

At starting rank 7 the established fit has three dead factors, two genomics-only programs (5 and 6), and two survival-active programs (3 and 7); the retained programs explain 1.9%–3.0% of the training variance each (S16, S58). Table 4 shows the starting-rank sweep. The evidence lower bound and BIC both prefer \(K_{\mathrm{init}} = 3\); the joint log-likelihood keeps rising to \(K_{\mathrm{init}} = 15\); cross-validated survival log partial likelihood is highest at 19; and external concordance is below 0.60 up to rank 6, then lies between 0.626 and 0.628 at every starting rank from 7 to 20 except 11 (0.600) and 13 (0.539). The number of survival-active programs is 1 at starting ranks 2–4 and 2 or 3 from rank 5 upward. Starting rank 7 is the smallest rank on the external-concordance plateau and the rank selected by training cross-validation (Section 1.4). The dated record attributes the dips at ranks 11 and 13 to single-start fitting failures, and an earlier explanation of the gap between ELBO and external performance in terms of reconstruction remains a hypothesis that was not verified (S01).

At starting rank 7 the classification is unchanged (two survival-active, two genomics-only) for coefficient thresholds from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-2}\) combined with PVE thresholds from 0.1% to 2%. A PVE threshold of 5% removes both genomics-only programs; a coefficient threshold of 0 counts four programs as survival-active because two coefficients are of order \(10^{-10}\); and a threshold of 0.05 counts none (S15).

3.4 Multimodal simulation

With pruning, the final number of programs depends much less on the starting rank (Figure 2). The original model has no removal step, so its final rank equals the starting rank in all 162 fits. At moderate noise the evaluated framework returns a mean of 3.2–3.3 programs in the two scenarios with high-variance prognostic programs and 2.5 in the low-variance scenario, averaged over starting ranks 3–15, and the means are close to constant from starting rank 4 upward. At the September noise level it returns fewer than three programs on average (1.7–2.0), and the final rank rises with the starting rank, from 1 at starting rank 3 to 2.3–3.3 at ranks 10 and 15; it is therefore not independent of the starting rank in that setting. All 162 fits of the evaluated framework met the convergence criterion, against 27 of 162 for the original model (S26).

Table 5 reports recovery by scenario and noise. At moderate noise, the framework recovers all three programs in the two-prognostic scenario and 2.96 of 3 in the adverse-and-protective scenario, finds 87% of prognostic programs with the correct sign, and has validation C of 0.79–0.80. In the low-variance scenario at moderate noise it recovers about two programs, finds the low-variance prognostic program in none of the 27 fits (recall 0), and classifies 1.26 other programs per fit as survival-active, so survival is attributed to high-variance programs; validation C is 0.63. At the September noise level, recovery is lower (0.93–1.33 programs), but the low-variance prognostic program is found in 52% of fits (48% with the correct sign). That result comes from a setting in which every true program is weak, so it does not show that the method recovers a low-variance program alongside strong ones. The variance-corrected survival term gave nearly identical results (largest difference in any summary in -mm-sim, 0.04). Each cell averages 27 fits from only three simulated datasets per setting, which limits precision.

3.5 Multimodal real-data validation

Table 6 compares models on the same 50 primary-PDAC ICGC donors and the 67-donor sensitivity set at starting rank 7. The joint expression-and-methylation fit has \(C = 0.685\) (0.579, 0.779) and the expression-only fit of the same framework \(C = 0.676\) (0.569, 0.770). Both fits stopped at the 500-sweep cap without meeting the convergence criterion. The difference of 0.010 is small relative to either interval and was not tested; similar observed concordance is not evidence of equivalence. On all 67 donors the order reverses (0.639 and 0.653). The two-step comparators have concordance below 0.53, and the September version of the joint model 0.453.

The October progress chapter (S39) reports that the established single-modality model has \(C = 0.685\) on the same 50 donors. That value is hard-coded in the plotting script, and no saved score file or computation was found for it during drafting, so it is not used here as a verified result; it appears in the evidence-gap table (Table 11). The established model was in any case trained on different data (TCGA and CPTAC, per-platform standardized, 2,064 genes), and the 50 donors overlap the PACA-AU RNA-seq cohort on which it was already evaluated.

Table 7 shows every starting rank. No factor was removed at any starting rank: the final rank equals the starting rank in all nine fits (S28). Only the fits at ranks 3 and 4 met the convergence criterion; the other seven stopped at the cap, and the removal check ran on those unconverged fits (Section 1.6). Concordance on the 50 primary donors ranges from 0.500 at rank 5, where no program is survival-active and every patient receives the same score, to 0.685 at rank 7; the median over the nine ranks is 0.572. The number of survival-active programs ranges from 0 to 11 and rises with the starting rank, while concordance does not. Rank 7 was chosen in advance as the single-modality default, but it is also the rank with the highest validation concordance in this sweep, so the headline rank-7 results are favourable relative to the other ranks.

The October progress chapter (S39) attributes the absence of pruning to each program’s molecular reconstruction gain being far larger than its complexity cost, with survival changing the evidence by at most a few units. That per-program decomposition was not traced to a saved output during drafting and is not quantified here. The plug-in survival term contributes on the scale of a 75-event partial likelihood, while the reconstruction term sums over \(144 \times 13{,}000\) molecular values, so in the evaluated objective survival can have little influence on which programs are retained.

4 Biological findings

4.1 Single-modality programs

The established fit retains four programs (Table 8). Each label below is tied to the analyses of Table 14 that support it. Two general points apply. First, the loadings of these programs were estimated without survival (\(\alpha_F = 0\)), so the biology describes the dominant expression structure of the training data, which survival then weights; it is not evidence of survival-guided discovery. Second, the normalized enrichment scores are modest (1.05–1.29 for the sets cited), the fgsea test is one-sided toward high loadings, and multiplicity is controlled only within each program and collection.

Program 7: adverse, basal-like. Its highest loadings combine glycolytic genes (GAPDH, ENO1, TPI1, PGK1, LDHA) with integrin and receptor-tyrosine-kinase genes (ITGA3, ITGB4, MET, CDCP1). Its enriched sets include DeSurv’s basal-like list (padj 0.0006), KEGG growth-factor RTK–PI3K and RAS–ERK pathways (padj 0.001) and Bailey squamous (padj 0.03) (S22). Training activities correlate with PurIST basal-like probability (\(\rho = 0.58\); S23); its top genes overlap only DeSurv’s basal-like list (Jaccard 0.18; S35); the basal-like signature has HR above 1 in all five external cohorts (1.30–2.40 per unit of mean score, \(p < 0.05\) in two; S24); and projection tertiles separate external survival (Figure 3). It corresponds to an unsupervised factor of the same data (\(r = 0.69\), next best 0.33; S45).

Program 3: protective, classical. The top genes are epithelial and secretory (CAPN5, LPCAT4, MLPH, SLC45A3, TJP3, GALNT6). The classical label rests mainly on subtype concordance (\(\rho = -0.58\)) and the classical signature’s HR below 1 in all five cohorts (0.42–0.88, \(p < 0.05\) in three). The enrichment is less specific: DeSurv’s classical and basal-like lists are both enriched (padj 0.017 each), with Moffitt classical and three integrin–FAK sets, and the top genes overlap both lists (Jaccard 0.13 and 0.10). Its unsupervised correspondence is less distinct (\(r = -0.72\), next best 0.60).

Program 5: genomics-only, desmoplastic stroma. Collagen and fibroblast genes dominate (COL1A2, COL3A1, COL5A2, THBS2, CDH11, SPARC); its twelve sets are led by Hallmark EMT (padj 0.0005), DeSurv’s stromal-immune list and extracellular-matrix organization; its top genes overlap only the stromal-immune list (Jaccard 0.18); it leans weakly basal (\(\rho = 0.30\)); and its EMT signature is not consistently prognostic externally (HR 0.73–1.50, \(p < 0.05\) in one cohort; S40).

Program 6: genomics-only, immune infiltrate with a vascular component. Lymphoid genes (IKZF1, AKNA, IL10RA, RCSD1, PREX1) are mixed with vascular and basement-membrane genes (APOLD1, COL14A1, TNXB, FBLN5, SLIT3, SPARCL1), so the label keeps both components, following the August 21 report (S21). Most of its 40 sets (S61) are immune GO terms, though the two lowest padj values are DeSurv’s classical and stromal-immune lists. It is uncorrelated with the PurIST axis (\(\rho = -0.03\)) but differs across PurIST calls (Kruskal–Wallis \(p = 0.007\)), a non-monotonic relation. Scored on its own immune set after the post hoc C4 correction, it has no consistent external association (HR 0.53–1.39, none with \(p < 0.05\); S40).

Together, the four programs map onto DeSurv’s three published factors, with DeSurv’s combined stromal-immune factor divided between a stromal and an immune program. This is gene-list correspondence within a DeSurv-aligned gene universe, not an independent replication of DeSurv and not a predictive comparison with it. The August 21 report also noted that the three dead programs have no enriched sets; their posterior-mean loadings are exactly zero in the saved fit, so that observation follows from the fit and does not corroborate the classification independently.

Direction labels. Adverse and protective labels follow the marginal association of each program’s projection with survival (S01). The pathway report read the stored coefficients (\(\tilde\beta_7 = -0.040\), \(\tilde\beta_3 = +0.012\)) as risk-scale values and described a sign disagreement with the marginal directions. Because the saved fit’s \(\eta\) is a good-prognosis score (Section 1.3.1), the risk-scale coefficients are \(+0.040\) for Program 7 and \(-0.012\) for Program 3, which agree in sign with the marginal labels. These coefficients are conditional on the other programs and are not interchangeable with the marginal associations.

4.2 Multimodal programs

The starting-rank-7 joint fit has seven programs (Table 9). Labels are provisional: they come from a manual reading of each program’s eight highest positive and six most negative expression loadings, together with the saved loading correlations to three references. No enrichment test and no CpG annotation was performed for these programs. Because the saved correlations are absolute values, the tables cannot show whether a matched pair points in the same direction, and best matches chosen independently for each program need not form a one-to-one alignment; for example, both the immune and stromal programs have their best established-model match in Program 6.

The one survival-active program (4) is the basal-like versus classical axis. Its marginal hazard ratio per SD of the joint projection is 1.99 in ICGC (\(p = 0.00033\)) and 1.34 in TCGA (\(p = 0.0055\)). It corresponds to established Program 7 (\(|r| = 0.68\)), and the classical/gastric program (1) corresponds to established Program 3 (\(|r| = 0.79\)), although Program 1 is not survival-active here. Of the 14 marginal tests, three have \(p < 0.05\) (Program 4 in both cohorts and Program 5 in TCGA); no correction for multiplicity was applied.

Methylation contributes in two ways (Figure 4). A methylation-only program carries 58.9% of the fitted methylation signal and has no expression loading. The immune program carries 20.9% of the methylation signal while being defined on the expression side by immune genes. Neither is survival-active, and neither has a marginal association with \(p < 0.05\). The basal-like program carries 4.5% of the methylation signal. These shares describe the fitted rank-one reconstruction within each modality. They are not additive proportions of variance, because cross-terms between programs are excluded, and they say nothing about each program’s contribution to survival prediction.

The current evidence therefore supports expression-defined program labels and the existence of methylation-dominant structure in the screened CpGs. It does not establish what that structure is. The 10,000 CpGs were chosen by variance, and high-variance CpGs often track cell composition, so the immune and methylation-only programs may reflect composition or technical variation; this is an explanation to test, not a finding.

5 Interpretation and remaining evidence

5.1 What the current evidence supports

The single-modality model yields a few interpretable programs and a risk score that transfers across platforms, but its advantage over a tuned two-step pipeline is small and marginal, and with \(\alpha_F = 0\) that advantage comes from how programs are fitted and coefficients shrunk, not from survival-guided discovery. Its programs match the known basal-like/classical and stromal/immune axes of PDAC. The multimodal framework fixes the September model’s failure to remove factors and works as designed in simulation when the true programs explain enough variance; on real data it has not shown that methylation improves prediction, nothing is pruned, and most fits are unconverged. Neither model recovers a planted low-variance prognostic program alongside strong ones, which is the case a supervised factorization exists for.

5.2 Evidence gaps by claim

Table 11 lists the six claims a manuscript would need to make, the evidence that exists, the conclusion it justifies now, and what is missing. It records the present state of the evidence; it does not imply that the missing analyses were run for this report.

5.3 Limitations

The external cohorts differ in platform, size and event rate, and two of them come from the same ICGC project; the matched multimodal validation set overlaps one of them. The multimodal real-data results rest on one training cohort of 144 patients with 75 deaths and a 50-donor validation set, so concordance intervals are wide (about \(\pm 0.10\)). Rank 7 is favourable among the multimodal starting ranks evaluated. The multimodal simulation uses three datasets per setting. Feature screening keeps 3,000 genes and the 10,000 highest-variance CpGs, about 3% of those available, and the effect of that choice is unknown. The single-modality simulation reports outcome-oriented concordance. The saved historical single-modality fit predates the September orientation correction and has no stored coefficient uncertainty. The biological characterization methods were chosen for availability and have not been assessed.

5.4 Continuing work

The configuration with \(\alpha_F = 0\) is not the intended final method: a supervised factorization should be able to find a prognostic program that explains little molecular variance, and the evaluated configuration cannot, because survival never enters the loading update. The planned work, recorded in the October 2 follow-up plan and its October 13 sequencing (S38), has five parts. These are plans; no result from them is reported here.

  1. Survival supervision of the loadings. Diagnose why survival has little effect even when it enters the loading update: its contribution is multiplied by the current coefficient, so a direction no program already points at receives no survival information; its precision is small relative to the reconstruction term; and in the single-modality model the loading scale is not fixed. The work adds the multimodal scale canonicalization to the single-modality model, removes \(\alpha_F\) as a separate setting, tests a supervised initialization, and compares a coefficient prior with an explicit survival weight. Success is defined in advance as recovery of a planted low-variance prognostic program in a large majority of simulation seeds, without instability and without loss of external concordance.
  2. Notation and prediction. Settle the definition of the normalized projection and the coefficient units once the scale canonicalization is in place, and carry the chosen supervision method into the multimodal model.
  3. Rank selection. Compare an evidence criterion with weighted survival against selection by cross-validated concordance plus reconstruction, with replicated simulation panels and a one-standard-error rule, for both models.
  4. Robustness and comparators. Repeat fits from jittered starts, compare loading prior families, vary the number of genes and CpGs, and run a comparator matrix in simulation and on real data that includes unsupervised factorization, the two-step pipeline, and DeSurv.
  5. Biology of the final programs. Recompute risk scores, survival curves and enrichment for the final programs, and add signed enrichment and CpG annotation for the multimodal programs.

References

Young, Amber M., Alisa Yurovsky, Xianlu Laura Peng, Jen Jen Yeh, Didong Li, and Naim U. Rashid. 2026. “Survival-Guided Matrix Factorization Identifies Reproducible Prognostic Programs in Pancreatic Cancer.” Unpublished manuscript.

Appendix A. Single-modality derivations

This appendix reconciles the existing single-modality derivations (S06, S07) with the evaluated D4 fit and the current implementation in code/fit_cox_on_yf.R and its update files (S04). It derives the updates the evaluated algorithm uses, states where the implementation departs from the joint mathematical model, and lists the approximations. Equation numbers continue from the main text.

A.1 Model and variational family

The joint model combines the reconstruction Equation 1 with a Cox model for \((t_i, \delta_i)\) whose linear predictor is \(\eta_i = \tilde z_i^\top\tilde\beta\), where \(\tilde z_i = D^{-1}\bar F^\top y_i\) is the normalized projection of Equation 2. Priors are \(L_{ik} \sim g_{L,k}\) and \(F_{jk} \sim g_{F,k}\) (point-exponential) and \(\tilde\beta_k \sim g_{\beta,k} = N(0, \sigma_k^2)\). The variational family is fully factorized, \[ q(L, F, \tilde\beta) = \prod_{i,k} q(L_{ik}) \prod_{j,k} q(F_{jk}) \prod_k q(\tilde\beta_k), \] with \(\tau\) and the prior parameters treated as point estimates. Write \(\bar L_{ik} = E_q L_{ik}\) and \(\overline{L^2}_{ik} = E_q L_{ik}^2\), and similarly for \(F\) and \(\tilde\beta\).

Two features of the predictor matter for every derivation below. First, \(\tilde z_i\) is formed from the posterior mean \(\bar F\), not from \(F\) itself, and \(D\) is computed from \(\bar F\) at the start of each outer iteration. The projection is therefore a fixed covariate within an iteration: it has no posterior variance in the coefficient update. Second, \(L\) does not appear in \(\eta\).

A.2 Cox working approximation

Let \(\hat\eta\) be the predictor at the start of an iteration, \(\hat\theta_i = \exp(\hat\eta_i)\), and \(\hat H_0\) the Breslow cumulative baseline hazard with ties sharing a risk-set denominator. The score and the diagonal of the negative Hessian of \(\log\mathrm{PL}\) with respect to \(\eta_i\) are approximated by \[ u_i = \delta_i - \hat\theta_i\hat H_0(t_i), \qquad w_i = \hat\theta_i\hat H_0(t_i), \tag{7}\] with \(w_i\) floored at \(10^{-6}\). A second-order expansion with this diagonal curvature gives \[ \log\mathrm{PL}(\eta) \approx c - \tfrac12\sum_i w_i (z_i - \eta_i)^2, \qquad z_i = \hat\eta_i + u_i / w_i. \tag{8}\] The exact Hessian of the partial likelihood is not diagonal; dropping its off-diagonal terms is the first approximation. When strata_id is supplied, risk sets and \(\hat H_0\) are formed within strata; the evaluated fit has no strata.

A.3 EBNM handoff

Every coordinate update below reduces to the same form. If the expected log objective, as a function of one scalar parameter \(\theta\), is \(B\theta - \frac12 A\theta^2 + \text{const}\) with \(A > 0\), it equals the log-likelihood of a single Gaussian observation \[ x = B/A, \qquad x \mid \theta \sim N(\theta, s^2), \qquad s = A^{-1/2}. \tag{9}\] The posterior under the prior \(g\) is the empirical-Bayes normal-means posterior for \((x, s)\), computed by ebnm, which also estimates \(g\) by marginal likelihood when \(g\) is shared across a vector of observations. The KL term needed for the objective follows from the identity \[ \mathrm{KL}(q \,\Vert\, g) = E_q\big[\log N(x; \theta, s^2)\big] - \log p(x), \tag{10}\] where \(p(x)\) is the marginal likelihood returned by ebnm.

A.4 Coefficient update

Isolate factor \(k\): \(\eta_i = \tilde Z_{ik}\tilde\beta_k + \eta_{i,-k}\), with \(\eta_{i,-k} = \sum_{l\ne k}\tilde Z_{il}\bar{\tilde\beta}_l\). Substituting into Equation 8 and taking the expectation over \(q(\tilde\beta_k)\) with \(\tilde Z\) fixed, the terms in \(\tilde\beta_k\) are \[ \tilde\beta_k \sum_i w_i \tilde Z_{ik}(z_i - \eta_{i,-k}) - \tfrac12\tilde\beta_k^2\sum_i w_i\tilde Z_{ik}^2 . \] The implementation multiplies the survival term by the weight \(\alpha\): \[ A_{\beta,k} = \alpha\sum_i w_i \tilde Z_{ik}^2, \qquad B_{\beta,k} = \alpha\sum_i w_i\tilde Z_{ik}(z_i - \eta_{i,-k}). \tag{11}\] The pseudo-observation \(B/A\) does not depend on \(\alpha\); its standard error is inflated by \(\alpha^{-1/2}\) (\(\sqrt 2\) at the evaluated \(\alpha = 0.5\)). The prior is normal with variance estimated by ebnm from this single pseudo-observation, which gives \(\hat\sigma_k^2 = \max(0, x^2 - s^2)\): a coefficient whose pseudo-observation is smaller than its standard error is set exactly to zero. With \(\tilde Z\) treated as fixed, Equation 11 uses \(\tilde Z_{ik}^2\) where the joint model would use \(E(\tilde Z_{ik}^2)\); posterior uncertainty in \(F\) does not reach the coefficient.

A.5 Activity update

Only the reconstruction term contains \(L\). With the factor-\(k\) residual \(R^{(-k)} = Y - \sum_{l\ne k}\bar L_{\cdot l}\bar F_{\cdot l}^\top\), the expected log-likelihood of Equation 1 contributes, for patient \(i\), \[ L_{ik}\sum_j \tau_j R^{(-k)}_{ij}\bar F_{jk} - \tfrac12 L_{ik}^2\sum_j\tau_j\overline{F^2}_{jk}, \] so \[ A_{L,k} = \sum_j \tau_j \overline{F^2}_{jk}, \qquad B_{L,ik} = \sum_j \tau_j R^{(-k)}_{ij}\bar F_{jk}, \tag{12}\] with one shared precision \(A_{L,k}\) across patients and a point-exponential prior fitted by ebnm over the \(n\) pseudo-observations. This is the standard empirical-Bayes matrix factorization update; it holds in every configuration of the single-modality model because \(\eta\) does not depend on \(L\).

A.6 Loading update

Reconstruction contribution. By the same argument as Equation 12 with the roles of \(L\) and \(F\) exchanged, \[ A^{\mathrm{gen}}_{F,jk} = \tau_j\sum_i\overline{L^2}_{ik}, \qquad B^{\mathrm{gen}}_{F,jk} = \tau_j\sum_i R^{(-k)}_{ij}\bar L_{ik}. \tag{13}\]

Survival contribution in the joint model. Because \(\eta\) depends on \(F\), the joint model also has a survival term in the loading update. Treating the normalizing constant \(d_k\) as fixed and writing \(\tilde Z_{ik} = d_k^{-1}\sum_j y_{ij}F_{jk}\), the terms of Equation 8 in \(F_{jk}\) are, up to factors of \(d_k\), \[ F_{jk}\,E(\tilde\beta_k)\sum_i w_i y_{ij}\big(z_i - \eta_{i,-k}\big) - \tfrac12 F_{jk}^2 E(\tilde\beta_k^2)\sum_i w_i y_{ij}^2 - F_{jk}E(\tilde\beta_k^2)\sum_i w_i y_{ij}\tilde Z^{(-j)}_{ik}, \] where the last term couples feature \(j\) to the other features through the projection excluding \(j\). A full treatment would also differentiate \(d_k\) with respect to \(F_{jk}\).

Implemented formula. update_F_surv_YFB_k() combines the two sources with weights \(1-\alpha_F\) and \(\alpha_F\): \[ A_{F,jk} = (1-\alpha_F)A^{\mathrm{gen}}_{F,jk} + \alpha_F E(\tilde\beta_k^2)\sum_i w_iy_{ij}^2, \quad B_{F,jk} = (1-\alpha_F)B^{\mathrm{gen}}_{F,jk} + \alpha_F E(\tilde\beta_k)\sum_i w_iy_{ij}(z_i - \eta_{i,-k}). \tag{14}\] This survival branch uses the unnormalized \(y_{ij}\), omits the feature-coupling term and the derivative of \(d_k\), and updates all features of factor \(k\) in one vectorized call. The plain Bayesian posterior corresponds to adding both sources with weight 1, which has the same pseudo-observation as \(\alpha_F = 0.5\) and twice its precision (S38). In the evaluated fit \(\alpha_F = 0\), so Equation 14 reduces to Equation 13 and the survival branch is not used. The F update is then the reconstruction update of empirical-Bayes matrix factorization, with the point-exponential prior fitted by ebnm over the \(p\) pseudo-observations.

A.7 Precision update

Maximizing the expected reconstruction log-likelihood over \(\tau_j\) gives \[ \tau_j = \frac{n}{\sum_i E_q\big(y_{ij} - L_i^\top F_j\big)^2}, \qquad E_q\big(y_{ij} - L_i^\top F_j\big)^2 = \big(y_{ij} - \bar L_i^\top\bar F_j\big)^2 + \sum_k\big(\overline{L^2}_{ik}\overline{F^2}_{jk} - \bar L_{ik}^2\bar F_{jk}^2\big), \tag{15}\] with a floor that bounds \(\tau_j\) by \(10^8\). There is no prior on \(\tau_j\).

A.8 Monitoring objective and stopping rule

After each outer iteration the implementation computes \[ J = (1-\alpha)\,G + \alpha\,p\,S + \sum_k\big(\kappa_{L,k} + \kappa_{F,k} + \kappa_{\beta,k}\big), \tag{16}\] where \(G = \sum_j\big[\frac n2\log\tau_j - \frac{\tau_j}{2}\sum_i E_q(y_{ij} - L_i^\top F_j)^2\big]\) is the reconstruction log-likelihood without its constant, \(S = \log\mathrm{PL}(\hat\eta) - \frac12\sum_i w_i\mathrm{Var}_q(\eta_i)\) with \(\mathrm{Var}_q(\eta_i) = \sum_k\tilde Z_{ik}^2\mathrm{Var}_q(\tilde\beta_k)\), and each \(\kappa\) is \(-\mathrm{KL}\) computed by Equation 10. The factor \(p\) comes from the per_p normalization convention, which scales only this monitored quantity. The algorithm stops at the first iteration after the fifth with \(|J_t - J_{t-1}|/|J_{t-1}| < 10^{-5}\). Because \(J\) weights its components by \(1-\alpha\) and \(\alpha p\), and because \(\log\mathrm{PL}\) is evaluated at the iteration’s starting predictor, \(J\) is a convergence monitor. It is not the evidence lower bound of the joint model, and the updates are not guaranteed to increase it.

A.9 Orientation and prediction

After the loop the implementation checks the training concordance of \(\eta\) once and negates \(\bar{\tilde\beta}\) if the score is discordant. Before September 4, 2026 this check omitted reverse = TRUE in survival::concordance(), so it was inverted, and it also replaced \(E(\tilde\beta^2)\) by \(E(\tilde\beta)^2\) when it negated. The saved D4 fit was produced by that code: its \(\eta\) is a good-prognosis score and its stored coefficient variances are zero. It is scored as \(\mathrm{risk} = -\eta\) for all held-out cohorts (S01, S49).

For a new patient with data standardized in its own cohort, prediction restricts \(\bar F\) to the training genes measured in that cohort but keeps the training normalizing constants \(D\), which were computed at the start of the final iteration: \(\eta_{\mathrm{new}} = y_{\mathrm{new}}^\top\bar F_{\mathcal{G}}D^{-1}\bar{\tilde\beta}\), where \(\mathcal{G}\) is the set of shared genes. Recomputing these projections from the saved fit reproduces the saved held-out scores to within \(10^{-8}\) (S49).

A.10 Mathematical model versus evaluated algorithm

The single-modality algorithm therefore performs exact coordinate updates of an empirical-Bayes factorization for \(L\), \(F\) and \(\tau\), interleaved with a plug-in empirical-Bayes update of the Cox coefficients on fixed projections. The derivation of a survival-informed loading update that is stable is part of the continuing work (Section 5.4).

Appendix B. Multimodal derivations

This appendix derives the updates of the evaluated multimodal framework (code/fit_multimodal_yfb.R and code/multimodal_yfb_updates.R; S08, S34) and reconciles them with the September base derivation (S33), which is preserved unchanged. The base derivation has nonnegative loadings, no intercept, moment-based prior updates, and no factor removal; the evaluated framework adds a feature intercept, signed point-Laplace loadings, marginal-likelihood prior fits, factor-scale canonicalization, and an evidence-based removal check. Its controls are those of the real-data runner (S29): intercept = TRUE, prior_F = point_laplace for both modalities, prior_update = "ebnm", tau_model = "feature", survival_elbo = "plugin", prune = TRUE, at most 500 outer sweeps of 5 inner sweeps, tolerance \(10^{-4}\).

B.1 Model

For modalities \(m \in \{\mathrm{expr}, \mathrm{meth}\}\), patients \(i\), features \(j\) and factors \(k\), \[ y_{mij} = \mu_{mj} + \sum_k l_{ik} f_{mjk} + e_{mij}, \qquad e_{mij} \sim N(0, \tau_{mj}^{-1}), \tag{17}\] \[ l_{ik} \sim g_{L,k} = (1-\pi_{L,k})\delta_0 + \pi_{L,k}\,\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_{L,k}), \qquad f_{mjk} \sim g_{mk} = (1-\pi_{mk})\delta_0 + \pi_{mk}\,\mathrm{Laplace}(0, \lambda_{mk}^{-1}), \tag{18}\] and \(\beta_k \sim N(0, \sigma_k^2)\). Survival follows a Cox model with \[ \eta_i = \sum_k Z_{ik}\beta_k, \qquad Z_{ik} = \sum_m\sum_j \tilde y_{mij} f_{mjk}, \qquad \tilde y_{mij} = y_{mij} - \mu_{mj}. \tag{19}\] The intercept \(\mu_{mj}\) and precision \(\tau_{mj}\) are point estimates. Because \(\sum_j \mu_{mj} f_{mjk}\) does not depend on \(i\), using \(y\) instead of \(\tilde y\) in Equation 19 changes every \(\eta_i\) by the same constant, which leaves the partial likelihood and the C-index unchanged. Signed loadings are needed because, with an intercept, \(f_{mjk}\) measures a deviation from the feature’s baseline and can be negative; \(L\) stays nonnegative and is read as program activity.

B.2 Variational family and objectives

The variational family is \(q = \prod_{i,k} q(l_{ik})\prod_{m,j,k} q(f_{mjk})\prod_k q(\beta_k)\). Two objectives are used. The removal objective is Equation 6: the reconstruction log-likelihood at the maximum-likelihood \(\hat\tau\), plus the Breslow log partial likelihood at \(E_q(\eta)\), minus the summed coordinate KL divergences computed by Equation 10. The coordinate updates use the Cox working surrogate at the predictor \(\hat\eta = E_q(\eta)\) from the start of the outer sweep, \[ \log\mathrm{PL}(\eta) \approx c + \sum_i\big(h_i\eta_i - \tfrac12 w_i\eta_i^2\big), \qquad h_i = u_i + w_i\hat\eta_i, \tag{20}\] which is Equation 8 rewritten (\(h_i = w_i z_i\)). The quantities \(w\) and \(h\) are held fixed for the five inner sweeps of an outer sweep. Its expectation under \(q\) is \(\sum_i\big[h_i E(\eta_i) - \frac12 w_i E(\eta_i^2)\big]\).

B.3 Intercept

At the start of each outer sweep, maximizing the expected reconstruction log-likelihood over \(\mu_{mj}\) gives \[ \hat\mu_{mj} = \frac1n\sum_i\Big(y_{mij} - \sum_k\bar l_{ik}\bar f_{mjk}\Big), \tag{21}\] and every block is re-centered, \(\tilde Y_m = Y_m - \mathbf 1\hat\mu_m^\top\). The survival term does not depend on \(\mu\) (B.1). The intercept is not updated within the inner sweeps. During the removal check it is re-estimated for each candidate set of factors, because deleting a nonnegative-activity factor moves its mean contribution into the intercept.

B.4 Projection and predictor moments

Under the mean-field posterior the loadings of different features are independent, so \[ E(Z_{ik}) = \sum_{m,j}\tilde y_{mij}\bar f_{mjk}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik}) = \sum_{m,j}\tilde y_{mij}^2\,\mathrm{Var}(f_{mjk}), \tag{22}\] and, with \(\beta\) independent of \(F\), \[ E(\eta_i) = \sum_k E(Z_{ik})\bar\beta_k, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\eta_i) = \sum_k\big[E(Z_{ik}^2)E(\beta_k^2) - E(Z_{ik})^2\bar\beta_k^2\big]. \tag{23}\] The implementation computes \(\mathrm{Var}(\eta_i)\) in the equivalent form \(\sum_k[\mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik})E(\beta_k^2) + E(Z_{ik})^2\mathrm{Var}(\beta_k)]\). The per-sweep diagnostic stored as fixed_working_objective uses a different expression that omits cross-factor terms of \(E(\eta_i^2)\); it is recorded for monitoring only and does not enter convergence, removal or any result in this report.

B.5 Shared activities

\(\eta\) does not depend on \(L\), so only the reconstruction terms of both blocks enter. With \(R^{(-k)}_m = \tilde Y_m - \sum_{l\ne k}\bar L_{\cdot l}\bar F_{ml}^\top\), \[ A_{L,k} = \sum_m\sum_j\tau_{mj}\overline{f^2}_{mjk}, \qquad B_{L,ik} = \sum_m\sum_j\tau_{mj}R^{(-k)}_{mij}\bar f_{mjk}. \tag{24}\] The posterior for each \(l_{ik}\) under the point-exponential prior, with \(x = B/A\) and \(s^2 = 1/A\), is a mixture of a point mass at zero and a normal distribution with location \(x - \lambda s^2\) truncated to \([0, \infty)\), with mixture weight proportional to \(\pi\lambda\exp(-\lambda x + \lambda^2 s^2/2)\Phi\big((x - \lambda s^2)/s\big)\) against \((1-\pi)N(x; 0, s^2)\). After the column update, \((\pi_{L,k}, \lambda_{L,k})\) is re-estimated by maximizing the marginal likelihood of the \(n\) pseudo-observations (ebnm_point_exponential, mode 0). Unlike a moment update, this fit can return the point mass (\(\pi = 0\)), which removes the column.

B.6 Modality-specific loadings

Reconstruction terms. As in Equation 13, \[ A^{\mathrm{rec}}_{mjk} = \tau_{mj}\sum_i\overline{l^2}_{ik}, \qquad B^{\mathrm{rec}}_{mjk} = \tau_{mj}\sum_i\bar l_{ik}R^{(-k)}_{mij}. \]

Survival terms and feature coupling. Write \(\eta_i = \beta_k Z_{ik} + \eta_{i,-k}\) and \(Z_{ik} = \tilde y_{mij}f_{mjk} + Z^{(-j)}_{ik}\), where \(Z^{(-j)}_{ik}\) collects every other feature of every modality. Substituting into the expected surrogate Equation 20 and keeping the terms in \(f_{mjk}\), \[ f_{mjk}\Big[\bar\beta_k\sum_i\tilde y_{mij}\big(h_i - w_iE\eta_{i,-k}\big) - E(\beta_k^2)\sum_i w_i\tilde y_{mij}E\big(Z^{(-j)}_{ik}\big)\Big] - \tfrac12 f_{mjk}^2\,E(\beta_k^2)\sum_i w_i\tilde y_{mij}^2 . \] The coefficient of \(f_{mjk}^2\) uses \(E(\beta_k^2)\) because \(\beta_k\) multiplies \(Z_{ik}\) in a squared term. Adding the reconstruction terms with equal weight, \[ A_{mjk} = \tau_{mj}\sum_i\overline{l^2}_{ik} + E(\beta_k^2)\sum_i w_i\tilde y_{mij}^2, \tag{25}\] \[ B_{mjk} = \tau_{mj}\sum_i\bar l_{ik}R^{(-k)}_{mij} + \bar\beta_k\sum_i\tilde y_{mij}h_{i,-k} - E(\beta_k^2)\sum_i w_i\tilde y_{mij}E\big(Z^{(-j)}_{ik}\big), \tag{26}\] with \(h_{i,-k} = h_i - w_iE(\eta_{i,-k})\). The last term couples feature \(j\) to all other features through the current projection: the survival information a feature receives depends on how much of the factor’s projection the other features already explain. Features are therefore updated sequentially (Gauss–Seidel). After each feature, \(E(Z_{\cdot k})\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Z_{\cdot k})\) are updated by the change in that feature’s moments, \(E(Z_{ik}) \mathrel{+}= \tilde y_{mij}(\bar f^{\mathrm{new}}_{mjk} - \bar f^{\mathrm{old}}_{mjk})\) and likewise for the variance. The survival terms are gated by \(\bar\beta_k\) and \(E(\beta_k^2)\): a factor with a coefficient near zero receives almost no survival information in its loadings (S38).

Point-Laplace posterior. With \(x = B/A\), \(s^2 = 1/A\), and prior \((1-\pi)\delta_0 + \pi\frac\lambda2 e^{-\lambda|f|}\), the posterior is a mixture of a point mass at zero, a positive part distributed as \(N(x - \lambda s^2, s^2)\) truncated to \(f > 0\), and a negative part distributed as \(N(x + \lambda s^2, s^2)\) truncated to \(f < 0\). Their log weights are \[ \log(1-\pi) + \log N(x; 0, s^2), \qquad \log\tfrac{\pi\lambda}{2} + \tfrac{\lambda^2s^2}{2} \mp \lambda x + \log\Phi\Big(\frac{\pm x - \lambda s^2}{s}\Big), \tag{27}\] and the posterior mean and second moment follow from truncated-normal moments (with an asymptotic expansion when the truncation point is far in the tail). These closed forms agree with ebnm at a fixed prior to \(10^{-6}\) (S01, 2026-10-01 entry). The point-Laplace parameters \((\pi_{mk}, \lambda_{mk})\) are held fixed during a modality–factor sweep and then re-estimated from that sweep’s \(p_m\) pseudo-observations by ebnm_point_laplace with mode 0. The stored KL values are those of the prior used in the sweep.

B.7 Survival coefficients

After the loadings of factor \(k\) are updated in both modalities, the terms of the expected surrogate in \(\beta_k\) are \(\beta_k\sum_iE(Z_{ik})h_{i,-k} - \frac12\beta_k^2\sum_iw_iE(Z_{ik}^2)\), so \[ A_{\beta,k} = \sum_iw_i\big[E(Z_{ik})^2 + \mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik})\big], \qquad B_{\beta,k} = \sum_iE(Z_{ik})\,h_{i,-k}. \tag{28}\] Unlike the single-modality update Equation 11, \(A_{\beta,k}\) includes the projection variance, so loading uncertainty shrinks the coefficient, and there is no \(\alpha\) weight. The prior variance is the single-observation marginal-likelihood estimate \(\hat\sigma_k^2 = \max(0, x^2 - 1/A)\) with \(x = B/A\). If \(\hat\sigma_k^2 = 0\), then \(q(\beta_k) = \delta_0\); otherwise \[ \mathrm{Var}(\beta_k) = \big(A_{\beta,k} + \hat\sigma_k^{-2}\big)^{-1}, \qquad \bar\beta_k = \mathrm{Var}(\beta_k)\,B_{\beta,k}, \] and \(\mathrm{KL} = \frac12\big[(\mathrm{Var}(\beta_k) + \bar\beta_k^2)/\hat\sigma_k^2 - 1 - \log(\mathrm{Var}(\beta_k)/\hat\sigma_k^2)\big]\). The survival-active classification uses \(|\bar\beta_k|/\mathrm{sd}(\beta_k) \ge 1.96\). The coefficients are initialized from a Cox fit on standardized initial projections, transformed back to the raw projection scale.

B.8 Precisions and expected squared residuals

After the inner sweeps, \[ \tau_{mj} = \frac{n}{\sum_iE_q\big(\tilde y_{mij} - l_i^\top f_{mj}\big)^2}, \qquad E_q\big(\tilde y_{mij} - l_i^\top f_{mj}\big)^2 = \big(\tilde y_{mij} - \bar l_i^\top\bar f_{mj}\big)^2 + \sum_k\big(\overline{l^2}_{ik}\overline{f^2}_{mjk} - \bar l_{ik}^2\bar f_{mjk}^2\big). \tag{29}\] These are unregularized maximum-likelihood values. Without an intercept, a spare factor could fit a single feature almost exactly and send its \(\tau_{mj}\) toward infinity, which made such factors impossible to remove; with the intercept this did not recur at moderate signal-to-noise (S01, 2026-10-01 entry). One precision per modality and a Gamma prior on \(\tau_{mj}\) are implemented alternatives that were not used in the evaluated fits.

B.9 Scale canonicalization

For any \(c_k > 0\), the map \((l_{\cdot k}, f_{mk}, \beta_k) \mapsto (c_kl_{\cdot k}, f_{mk}/c_k, c_k\beta_k)\) leaves \(LF_m^\top\) and \(\eta\) unchanged. The likelihood therefore does not fix the scale of a factor, and coordinate updates can move along this direction; in the single-modality model with survival in the loading update this caused a runaway (S38). After each factor’s coefficient update the implementation sets \(c_k = \mathrm{sd}(E Z_{\cdot k})\) over training patients and applies the map, transforming the other quantities consistently: \[ \overline{l^2}_{\cdot k} \mapsto c_k^2\,\overline{l^2}_{\cdot k}, \quad \overline{f^2}_{mk} \mapsto \overline{f^2}_{mk}/c_k^2, \quad E(\beta_k^2) \mapsto c_k^2E(\beta_k^2), \quad \lambda_{L,k} \mapsto \lambda_{L,k}/c_k, \quad \lambda_{mk} \mapsto c_k\lambda_{mk}. \tag{30}\] (A normal loading prior variance would map to \(\sigma^2/c_k^2\).) The prior rates transform so that the prior probability of each transformed coordinate is unchanged. After canonicalization, \(\mathrm{sd}(EZ_{\cdot k}) = 1\) in training, so a coefficient is per training standard deviation of the joint projection. The step does not change the fitted reconstruction or predictor, but it is applied between coordinate updates and therefore changes the path of the algorithm.

B.10 Stopping rule

At the end of each outer sweep the algorithm computes, for each modality, \(\max|\Delta(\bar L\bar F_m^\top)| / \max(1, \max|\bar L\bar F_m^\top|)\) and the same quantity for \(E(\eta)\), and stops when all are below \(10^{-4}\). These quantities are invariant to the scale exchange of B.9, which is why they are used instead of changes in posterior moments. The cap is 500 outer sweeps. In the real-data sweep only the fits at starting ranks 3 and 4 met the criterion (S28).

B.11 Removal check and refitting

When the coordinate loop ends, whether by meeting the criterion or by reaching the cap, the removal check computes, for each factor \(k\), \[ \Delta_k = \mathcal E\big(\text{factors} \ne k\big) - \mathcal E\big(\text{all factors}\big), \tag{31}\] where \(\mathcal E\) is Equation 6 evaluated with factor \(k\)’s activities, loadings and coefficient set to zero, its KL terms removed, the other factors’ posteriors held fixed, and \(\mu\) and \(\tau\) re-estimated. If \(\max_k\Delta_k \ge 0\), the factor with the largest \(\Delta_k\) is deleted, the algorithm restarts from the remaining factors’ moments and priors (a warm start with \(K - 1\) factors), and the check repeats after that fit. Holding the other factors fixed makes the check conservative: a deletion is accepted only if the evidence does not fall even before the remaining factors adapt. The removal history records whether each fit was converged when it was checked.

The survival component of \(\mathcal E\) is \(\log\mathrm{PL}(E\eta)\), whereas the exact variational objective would use \(E_q\log\mathrm{PL}(\eta)\). Because the log partial likelihood is concave in \(\eta\), Jensen’s inequality gives \(E_q\log\mathrm{PL}(\eta) \le \log\mathrm{PL}(E\eta)\): the plug-in overstates the survival term, by an amount that grows with \(\mathrm{Var}(\eta)\). A second-order correction gives \(\log\mathrm{PL}(E\eta) - \frac12\sum_iw_i\mathrm{Var}(\eta_i)\), the corrected option; in the simulation sweep it changed no summary by more than 0.04 (Section 3.4). Neither form makes \(\mathcal E\) a guaranteed lower bound on the marginal likelihood, and the coordinate updates are not guaranteed to increase it. On real data the reconstruction component, which sums over every feature of both modalities, dominates \(\mathcal E\), so survival has little influence on which factors are kept.

B.12 Prediction

For a new patient with features aligned to the training features, \(\eta_{\mathrm{new}} = \sum_m y_{m,\mathrm{new}}^\top\bar F_m\bar\beta\), using raw (uncentered) data; centering at the training intercept would shift every score by the same constant. Orientation is fixed from training (flip = FALSE): higher \(\eta\) means higher risk.
